question.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x),$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x).$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x)}{{e}^{-x}+{e}^{x}} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x+p & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x & =-p.\end{aligned}
$$
